title: Safeguarding concerns, community costs and fireworks raised at Rochdale council meeting
excerpt: Farooq Ahmed raised concerns about safeguarding powers, while Jordan Tarrant-Short questioned venue costs, fireworks, foster care and Warwick Mill at full council.
body:
Concerns about the potential misuse of safeguarding powers, community venue charges and fireworks nuisance were raised during Rochdale’s full council meeting on Thursday, October 15.

Councillor Farooq Ahmed questioned how the council prevented staff from overstepping their authority, while Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short pressed cabinet members on issues including foster-carer recruitment, Warwick Mill and access to community facilities.

Councillors also rejected a proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments and backed motions concerning energy costs in new homes, protecting pubs and condemning attacks on places of worship.

Concern over safeguarding powers

Ahmed stressed that protecting vulnerable adults and children must come first, but questioned whether safeguarding procedures could sometimes harm the people they were intended to protect.

He said some officers could overstep their authority, leaving service users and families feeling victimised. He suggested the term safeguarding could be abused and asked how the council ensured staff did not misuse their powers.

Councillor Shah Wazir said safeguarding should protect and support people without causing avoidable distress. He outlined expectations around involving residents in decisions, providing advocacy where required and reviewing complaints and practice.

Responding to Ahmed’s supplementary question, Wazir invited him to provide specific incidents and promised they would be examined. The mayor also encouraged Ahmed to report his concerns.

The exchange raised concerns about potential misuse; it did not establish that misconduct had occurred in any particular case.

Community groups facing venue costs

Tarrant-Short said community organisations had contacted him about hire charges at facilities managed by Your Trust, warning that costs could make their activities financially unsustainable.

He told the meeting that a local dance group had reported being quoted £11,000 for one evening at Heywood Civic Centre. The booking requirements and an explanation of that reported quotation were not established during the exchange.

He asked whether protections, concessions or community pricing policies could prevent voluntary organisations being priced out.

Councillor Sue Smith said reduced rates or room-hire waivers could be available where appropriate, but charges also had to cover staffing, technical support and other operating costs.

She asked him to send details so officers could investigate. Smith said she had helped groups reduce charges, sometimes through changes to booking dates or times, but did not announce a new borough-wide pricing policy.

Fireworks and stronger safeguards

Tarrant-Short raised residents’ concerns about fireworks being used throughout the year, describing distress to families, vulnerable people and pets.

He asked what action the council and partner agencies were taking, then pressed for lobbying for stronger regulation and enforcement powers.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton acknowledged the concerns and said she had been speaking with partner agencies about a coordinated response.

She also said the council’s three community bonfire events would use reduced-noise fireworks, accompanied by music and lights. In response to his request for stronger national action, she encouraged councillors to raise concerns with their MPs.

Recruiting and retaining foster carers

Tarrant-Short asked how the council would increase the number of local foster carers and provide enough family placements for vulnerable children.

Councillor Rachel Massey outlined work through the Greater Manchester fostering recruitment hub, alongside specialist fostering, training and support. She identified particular needs for carers supporting teenagers, sibling groups and children with disabilities.

In a supplementary question, Tarrant-Short congratulated the children’s services team before asking what recruitment targets would replace retiring carers and increase overall capacity.

Massey said recruitment strategies and targets existed, while stressing the importance of finding the right home for each child. She did not give a numerical recruitment target in that exchange.

Warwick Mill and local investment

Tarrant-Short asked whether Warwick Mill would be acquired through compulsory purchase.

Council leader Neil Emmott said the council had negotiated an agreement with the owner and that cabinet had approved exercising an option to purchase following due diligence.

Asked why decisive intervention had taken so long, Emmott pointed to private ownership and previous unsuccessful redevelopment proposals, saying the council was now taking action.

Tarrant-Short also called for more community events in Rochdale South, including his Balderstone and Kirkholt ward.

Later, he asked whether a previously discussed highways review meeting had taken place. Scrutiny chair Councillor Tom Besford said no date had yet been arranged and promised to follow it up with him.

Pub protections and council votes

Tarrant-Short formally moved an amendment to the pub-protection motion, which councillors approved unanimously. The amended motion subsequently passed, supporting action over restrictive covenants that can prevent former pubs reopening.

Councillors unanimously supported motions on reducing energy costs in new homes and condemning attacks on places of worship.

A proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments was defeated.
